subtitle: The iceberg image helps you separate what you can observe from the meanings beneath the surface that you still need to understand, a useful habit before drawing conclusions.
scope: For staff across DHS. The iceberg is a learning metaphor, not a diagnostic instrument, a percentage measure of culture or an IDI assessment. Use invented or appropriately shareable situations and keep private client, personnel and medical information out of course activities. Actual policy, accommodation and workplace concerns retain their responsible routes. Matters involving Native American communities or Tribal relations should be referred to the appropriate office within ADSA.
introTranscript: The cultural iceberg can be a useful reminder that what we see does not reveal every meaning behind an interaction. It can also mislead if we treat its hidden portion as permission to guess motives or assign group traits. In this course you will use the image carefully: describe an observation, identify your interpretation, consider more than one possibility and ask an appropriate question. The later lessons apply the same reasoning to a meeting and a service communication. The goal is a more accurate work response, not a profile of another person’s hidden culture.

intro.heading: Read the image without turning it into a measurement
intro.body:
The iceberg image contrasts a visible part with a less apparent part. Peace Corps educational material uses it to introduce observable cultural features and meanings that may not be immediately visible. In this course, the useful distinction is between what you can describe and what you still need to understand. The image is a way to organize thought, not an instrument that reveals a person’s internal world.

A literal iceberg has physical properties. Culture does not therefore have a measured visible-to-hidden percentage. Do not turn a number associated with the picture into a scientific statement about how much of an employee’s culture you can see. The metaphor also does not mean that every action has a single hidden cultural cause. A response can involve a task, access, available information, individual experience and several other influences.

Imagine a practice meeting where a participant looks at a draft and says little. The observation belongs above the line: few comments were made during that meeting. Beneath the line you might place questions about meaning, preparation or expectations. You should not write that the person opposes the proposal or belongs to a particular IDI orientation. Those are conclusions the observation cannot establish.

Use the image as a reminder to slow down an interpretation. Describe what happened, name the explanation you supplied and decide what evidence or appropriate question could help. If the issue has an immediate formal responsibility, follow it rather than extending a learning exercise. Thoughtful curiosity is useful when it improves the next work step; it is not permission to delay a necessary response.

flashcards.back: An image that distinguishes readily observed features from meanings and expectations that may not be apparent.
A description of an action, object, word or arrangement available to examine.
A proposed explanation that remains uncertain until relevant evidence supports it.
Treating your own meaning or expectation as though another person must share it.
A neutral question about the present situation that allows a person to explain without representing a group.
A clear statement of what the available information cannot establish.

items.title: A reminder to examine meaning
items.body: In a practice project meeting, a participant gives few comments. The image can remind the facilitator to ask whether the material and question were usable. That is a practical inquiry. It cannot determine the participant’s motivation or establish the values of everyone with a similar background.

items.title: A picture mistaken for data
items.body: A facilitator says that the diagram proves a precise percentage of culture is hidden. The drawing does not provide a measurement method or dataset for that claim. Present the above-and-below distinction as a metaphor and return to the actual evidence available about the interaction.

items.title: A hidden portion mistaken for a diagnosis
items.body: An observer fills the lower section with an employee’s supposed cultural stage. Nothing in the metaphor authorizes that assessment. Keep it to possible meanings and evidence questions. Official IDI assessment remains separate, and course activity should not create a personal developmental label.

tabs.label: Helpful use
tabs.body: The image can interrupt the belief that an observed action explains itself. It invites a question about meaning or an overlooked condition. For the quiet meeting participant, the next step might be checking the review instructions. The usefulness comes from a better inquiry, not a fuller-looking drawing.

tabs.label: Overextended use
tabs.body: The image becomes misleading when its lower section is treated as a discovered list of traits. A confident explanation can feel complete while being entirely assumed. Filling it with a nationality-based claim or inferred orientation turns a learning metaphor into a profile without a valid assessment or relevant evidence.

tabs.label: Bounded use
tabs.body: Name the observation, mark possibilities as uncertain and choose a work-relevant question. This allows the metaphor to support a practical response while keeping its limits visible. If the inquiry reveals an access request or formal concern, use its responsible route rather than trying to solve it inside the diagram.

check.question: What does the cultural iceberg establish about a quiet meeting participant?
check.correct: It can remind you that the visible response has meanings or conditions you have not established.
wrong: It reveals a precise percentage of the person’s hidden culture.
It proves that their community discourages disagreement.
check.feedbackCorrect: This uses the image to question an interpretation while retaining the limits of the observation.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The drawing does not measure an individual’s culture. A community explanation is not established by one quiet response. An IDI orientation cannot be inferred from the diagram or a meeting. Treat the lower portion as questions and possibilities, then examine the actual situation and work need.

items.text: Few comments were made during the meeting.
The participant may need more time to examine the draft.
The diagram proves the person’s developmental orientation.
The draft was shown only after the meeting began.
The review expectation may not have been clear.
A specific percentage of this person’s culture is hidden.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: Facilitator Ian shows an iceberg diagram after a practice briefing meeting. Bea made few comments. Ian says the lower section reveals her hidden orientation and writes a cultural percentage next to her name.
options: Keep the labels because the image makes them easier to understand.
Use the image to identify uncertain meaning and work questions, removing the percentage and personal assessment claims.
Assume quiet participation has no meaning worth examining.
responses: A clear image cannot validate an unsupported personal claim.
This preserves the useful distinction without pretending the image measured or assessed Bea.
Rejecting every inquiry loses the chance to examine the actual work opportunity.

lessons.transfer: Draw or describe a practice iceberg with one observation, two questions and one explicit limit. Do not put a real person’s name in it.

move.control: You can use a metaphor to organize a question without treating it as evidence.
move.failure: An educational image becomes a scientific-looking personal label.
move.next: When presenting the iceberg, explain what it can help ask and what it cannot establish.

takeaways: Start with words, actions and arrangements.
An observation has a scope and context.
lessons.statement: An accurate surface description makes the next question more useful.

intro.heading: Describe the surface before explaining what is below it
intro.body:
A statement can look like an observation while already carrying a judgment. “The person was disrespectful” does not tell another reader what occurred. “The person asked why the evidence source was excluded” describes a question that can be examined. The first statement may eventually be supported by relevant conduct evidence, but it should not replace that evidence at the start of an inquiry.

Describe the feature with enough context to be useful. In a practice draft discussion, record that a colleague asked a question before the presenter finished explaining the criteria. Note the question and the arrangement rather than guessing the colleague’s intent. It may be relevant that the meeting invited questions throughout, or that no opportunity had been announced. The same action can have a different work effect in a different setting.

Separate the event, its possible effect and your evaluation. A question may interrupt the sequence, identify a missing assumption or do both. Naming that effect does not require a personality judgment. Ask what requirement or expectation applies before deciding that the action violated it. Respectful conduct remains important, and actual concerns belong in their applicable processes.

Keep information proportionate. A learning note needs an example, not a real personnel transcript or a private client account. The purpose of describing the surface is to make reasoning examinable. It is not to build a new collection of employee behavior. If a formal record is required, use its approved procedure rather than a course response. A clear observation helps you locate the question while preserving authority and privacy.

lessons.keyStatement: An accurate surface description makes the next question more useful.

items.title: A label that seems obvious
items.body: “Dismissive” may be the reader’s sincere impression, but it does not show the action. In a practice discussion, identify the words, timing and response opportunity. That detail lets someone examine whether an important concern was raised respectfully, poorly handled or misunderstood. It does not automatically excuse the conduct.

items.title: Context that changes the account
items.body: A participant interrupts during an announced open-question section. Calling that an interruption without the arrangement can mislead. Describe the invitation and actual effect. If the meeting instead reserved questions until the end, note that distinction before explaining the response or proposing a better participation route.

items.title: An effect without a personality claim
items.body: An early question may prevent the presenter from completing a comparison. State that effect and clarify the agreed discussion approach. You can preserve the work sequence without saying that the person’s identity makes them impatient. A process response can address the event while leaving motive uncertain.

tabs.label: Label
tabs.body: A label compresses an interpretation, often with little evidence visible. “Uncooperative” can refer to many different actions and may stop the inquiry too soon. Ask which specific behavior or work result supports it. If you cannot explain that basis, the label belongs among interpretations to examine.

tabs.label: Description
tabs.body: A description states what happened and enough context to understand its limits. For example, a participant questioned an excluded source during the open-question period. This gives the next reader something concrete to examine without claiming to know motive or treating a group identity as the explanation.

tabs.label: Work effect
tabs.body: A work effect connects the event to the task, such as a missing source being reviewed or a sequence being delayed. It should be supported and proportionate. An effect can justify a practical adjustment while leaving intent uncertain; a formal conduct question still follows its designated process.

check.question: Which statement best describes a practice meeting observation?
check.correct: A participant asked why one source was excluded during the announced question period.
wrong: The participant’s background made them disrespectful.
They wanted to embarrass the presenter.
Their question proves they cannot collaborate.
check.feedbackCorrect: The statement describes a question and its participation context without inserting a motive or group explanation.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A background claim does not show the conduct. An embarrassment motive cannot be read directly from the question. Declaring inability to collaborate turns one event into a broad personal conclusion. Describe the words and situation, then examine the relevant work effect and expectation.

items.text: The participant asked which evidence supported option two.
They asked only to undermine the presenter.
The meeting invited questions during the comparison.
The presenter answered after the question.
Their identity makes them incapable of teamwork.
The source list had not been shared before the meeting.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: During a practice open-question period, Milan asks why a source was excluded. Cara writes “Milan is culturally confrontational” in her private learning draft. The source list had not been available before the meeting.
options: A description of the question and context, followed by an evidence question about its work effect.
A stronger cultural trait claim to make the point clear.
Nothing, because every difficult exchange is harmless.
responses: This makes the event examinable without profiling Milan or assuming the question’s motive.
A stronger claim supplies no additional evidence and broadens the unsupported judgment.
Clear description can preserve a real work concern without declaring every exchange harmless.

lessons.transfer: Rewrite three practice labels as observations with context. Mark any evaluation or motive still needing evidence.

move.control: You can make the account specific and proportionate before acting on an interpretation.
move.failure: A surface label carries an assumed motive into every later decision.
move.next: Before explaining an interaction, identify the actual words, arrangement and work effect.

lessons.title: Consider more than one explanation beneath the surface

Cultural meaning is one possibility, not the only possibility.
A useful explanation can be checked and revised.
lessons.statement: Keep the lower section open to evidence rather than filling it with the first story that feels right.

intro.heading: Consider more than one explanation beneath the surface
intro.body:
The hidden portion of the iceberg can encourage curiosity, but it can also become a space for confident guesses. An observer may supply a cultural explanation because it is the topic of the course. That is an example of choosing the answer before examining the situation. Ask which alternatives fit the available facts and what evidence could distinguish them.

In a practice review, a colleague does not respond to a same-day request. Possible explanations include workload, an unclear question, lack of access to the draft, a belief that another role should answer or a personal communication preference. A cultural expectation may be relevant, but the response alone cannot show that it is the cause. Nor does listing possibilities establish that every explanation is equally likely.

Choose a proportionate way to investigate the work question. Check whether the message and draft were available, whether the response time was explained and whether the colleague understood the decision needed. A neutral question can invite relevant information without asking for private family, medical or identity details. The evidence you need may be about the arrangement rather than the person’s background.

Revise the account when evidence changes it. If the draft link was unavailable, that fact can support an access repair. It does not prove that no other issue mattered. If a colleague describes a meaning you had not considered, keep it scoped to their account. Multiple explanations are a discipline for avoiding premature closure; they are not an excuse to remain indecisive when a clear action or formal duty is required.

Distinguish a testable question from an invented hidden trait.
Identify evidence that could change an initial interpretation.
Which action best fits the uncertainty?
lessons.keyStatement: Keep the lower section open to evidence rather than filling it with the first story that feels right.

items.title: The first explanation feels persuasive
items.body: A staff member interprets a delayed response as disrespect for urgency. Check the message, expectation and draft access before acting on that story. Familiar interpretations can feel self-evident precisely because they match the observer’s habits. A concrete evidence question makes them open to correction.

items.title: Culture becomes the automatic cause
items.body: Because this is a culture course, someone puts culture under every observed action. That turns the lesson into a fixed answer key. Ask what other task, access or context explanations fit the event. Cultural meaning can still matter, but the inquiry must establish its relevance rather than assume it.

items.title: Possibilities replace action
items.body: Listing six explanations without checking any can leave a blocked task unchanged. Choose an appropriate next question or evidence check and assign the work owner. If a formal concern arises, follow its route immediately where required. Uncertainty is a reason for careful action, not indefinite postponement.

tabs.label: One story
tabs.body: One story can create speed and confidence, but it may explain only the observer’s expectations. Calling nonresponse disrespectful skips whether the message was usable or the timing agreed. A response based on that story can create conflict while leaving the actual task dependency unresolved.

tabs.label: Several possibilities
tabs.body: Several possibilities keep the account open and help identify missing evidence. They should be plausible and connected to the facts, not a catalogue of private guesses. Compare a workload or access explanation with a meaning question, then decide which information would most usefully guide the next work step.

tabs.label: Evidence and revision
tabs.body: A useful check can support one explanation and weaken another. If the link was unavailable, repair access and confirm the next step. Keep any remaining uncertainty visible instead of claiming a complete cultural explanation. The ability to revise reasoning is more useful than filling every blank in the picture.

check.question: A colleague did not answer a practice same-day draft request. What is the strongest next inquiry?
check.correct: Check message access, stated timing and the work question, then ask for relevant clarification without assuming a cultural cause.
wrong: Decide their community does not value deadlines.
Collect their private medical history to find the cause.
List possibilities indefinitely without addressing the blocked task.
check.feedbackCorrect: This tests relevant conditions and creates an actionable inquiry without unnecessary personal information.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A community deadline claim is unsupported by the response. Private medical collection is not the ordinary evidence needed to check a message and review route. Endless possibility listing leaves the task blocked. Examine proportionate work information, clarify what remains uncertain and choose the next action within responsibility.

items.text: Was the requested response timing explained?
Their community never values deadlines.
Confirm whether the approved draft link worked.
Did the colleague understand who should answer?
Silence establishes a fixed cultural orientation.
Check which information was available when the request was sent.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: Evan receives no answer to a practice draft request and says the colleague’s culture explains it. The link was sent that morning, and the response expectation was not stated. The draft still needs review.
scenario.prompt: Which action best fits the uncertainty?
options: Treat the cultural explanation as established.
Ask for an identity profile before repairing the link.
Check access and the decision question, explain an appropriate response route and timing, and revise the interpretation as evidence arrives.
responses: The observation has not established the proposed cause.
The immediate work information can be checked without a complete private identity account.
This turns uncertainty into a proportionate inquiry and a usable next step.

lessons.transfer: For a practice delayed response, name three plausible explanations, the smallest useful evidence check and what its result would not establish.

move.control: You can keep interpretations open while taking a proportionate practical step.
move.failure: A hidden story is treated as confirmed, or uncertainty becomes an excuse to do nothing.
move.next: Ask what evidence could change your first interpretation before relying on it.

lessons.objective: Write a neutral meaning question tied to the present task.
objectives: Write a neutral meaning question tied to the present task.
Distinguish voluntary explanation from a representative burden.
Respond to a person’s account without generalizing it to a group.
takeaways: Ask about the situation rather than presumed group traits.
People choose which personal information to share.
One account can clarify an interaction without explaining everyone.
lessons.statement: A meaning question creates space for an answer; it should not dictate the story the person must tell.

image.caption: Colleagues share information and consider a decision together.

intro.heading: Ask about meaning without demanding a personal account
intro.body:
A question can appear curious while carrying an assumption. “Why do people like you avoid disagreement?” assumes the observed person avoided disagreement, supplies a group explanation and asks them to represent that group. A neutral question focuses on the situation: which part of the draft needs further examination, or what would make the response route useful? That wording leaves room for meaning without insisting on an identity story.

Explain why you are asking and connect the question to the work. In a practice meeting, a facilitator might ask whether participants have enough information to compare two options. The question is useful because the decision depends on their review. It should not become a public demand that a quiet colleague justify their personal style or disclose circumstances.

Listen to the account actually offered. A person may explain that a written comment lets them distinguish evidence from uncertainty. You can discuss whether that method fits the task and appropriate timing. Do not turn their explanation into a rule that everyone from a presumed community should write instead of speak. Shared cultural patterns and individual experience remain different kinds of information.

Allow the person to decline personal elaboration and choose another evidence route where appropriate. You may be able to inspect the instructions or improve the review channel without their identity account. Power matters: an employee may feel unable to refuse a supervisor’s request. Keep optional learning separate from performance expectations and formal procedures. Curiosity should reduce confusion while respecting the person’s choice about what is relevant.

Distinguish voluntary explanation from a representative burden.
Respond to a person’s account without generalizing it to a group.

lessons.keyStatement: A meaning question creates space for an answer; it should not dictate the story the person must tell.

items.title: A neutral task question
items.body: Ask which information a colleague needs to compare the options. This does not rule out a cultural meaning; it leaves the explanation open. If the answer identifies a missing assumption, address that work feature. The useful result is clearer participation, not proof of how the person’s community thinks.

items.title: A request made in public
items.body: A facilitator singles out a participant to explain why their group is quiet. Even if kindly intended, the request can impose an identity and representative burden. Offer a general usable response opportunity and established learning resources instead of requiring one employee to supply the team’s cultural education.

items.title: A scoped voluntary account
items.body: A colleague voluntarily explains a communication experience. Preserve the meaning and scope of that account, and do not circulate private details beyond their appropriate setting. Ask what work adjustment follows, if any. Learning from someone does not make their experience a universal rule or a new personnel label.

tabs.label: Leading question
tabs.body: A leading question embeds the observer’s explanation in its wording. Asking why a group dislikes debate assumes a pattern and makes the person defend it. An answer obtained under that premise can look like evidence while reflecting pressure to respond to the story already supplied.

tabs.label: Neutral question
tabs.body: A neutral question identifies the actual uncertainty and permits more than one answer. Ask what information or participation route is needed for this decision. Explain the purpose and avoid unnecessary disclosure. This keeps curiosity useful and allows a practical response even when cultural identity is not the relevant issue.

tabs.label: Scoped response
tabs.body: A scoped response uses the person’s account for the present interaction and preserves its limits. If a written route supports their analysis, examine its timing and usefulness without assigning it to every colleague with a similar identity. Their explanation adds understanding; it does not authorize a group profile.

check.question: Which question best fits an uncertain response during a practice draft review?
check.correct: What information or response arrangement would help you examine these options?
wrong: Why is your whole community uncomfortable with questions?
What personal history must you disclose to prove you belong here?
Which cultural stage explains your quietness?
check.feedbackCorrect: The question is connected to the decision and allows relevant meaning without an identity test or personal assessment.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A community question assumes the cause and assigns representation. Requiring personal history turns learning into a belonging test. An inferred stage is not available from quietness or this activity. Ask about the current work need and respect the person’s choice about a personal account.

items.text: Which part of the instruction needs clarification?
Explain why everyone in your community acts that way.
Use a voluntary account to clarify this interaction without generalizing it.
What response route would support the review task?
Prove your cultural identity before we consider the comment.
Discuss the work effect while keeping private details appropriately handled.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: Facilitator Mae wants to understand why participant Luca sent a written comment. She begins with a question about his entire community. Luca would rather discuss the source comparison he completed.
options: What made the written comment useful for this source review, and what arrangement supports the next step?
Which identity explains Luca’s behavior in every meeting?
Why Luca refuses to teach the team about his background.
responses: This invites the relevant meaning and allows a practical discussion without imposing representation.
A single identity cannot establish every interaction or replace the current question.
Declining an identity account is not refusal to contribute to the work.

lessons.transfer: Rewrite two leading questions as neutral task questions. Add how you would respect a declined personal explanation.

move.control: You can ask for relevant meaning without making a personal account compulsory.
move.failure: Curiosity becomes a public identity test or a requirement to speak for a group.
move.next: Before asking about meaning, check whether the question already assumes the answer.

lessons.statement: The iceberg can help reveal your process assumptions rather than treating other people as the hidden problem.

image.caption: Colleagues share information and consider a decision together.

intro.heading: Use the image to examine a process, not only a person
intro.body:
The iceberg is often aimed at another person: their visible action and their supposed hidden values. Turning it toward a work arrangement can be more useful. A meeting format, response channel or review invitation can rest on expectations that its designers never explained. You can examine those assumptions without profiling the people who encounter them.

Consider a practice review that shows a long draft only during the meeting and requests immediate comments. The visible arrangement is the timing and response method. The less apparent assumption may be that everyone can examine the evidence and formulate a useful question at once. A participant’s quietness then becomes a clue to examine the arrangement, not proof of a personal cultural deficit.

Compare an option with the work purpose and constraints. Sharing an approved draft earlier may create time for review. A written question route may preserve analysis that would otherwise arrive too late. Both require the correct version, appropriate access, a decision question and someone who will respond. Do not waive information permissions or a formal review requirement because an option seems more inclusive.

Check the tradeoff. A new route may increase review burden or fragment comments unless the owner explains how it works. Make the response arrangement clear and examine whether meaningful information reaches the decision before it closes. The proposed change should address a supported assumption, not a claim that a certain community always needs a particular method. Consultant guidance can strengthen the inquiry while staff carry out the work within their roles.

lessons.keyStatement: The iceberg can help reveal your process assumptions rather than treating other people as the hidden problem.

items.title: A default beneath the meeting
items.body: Immediate response can feel natural to a team accustomed to seeing familiar material. A complex new draft may need another review opportunity. Examine the purpose and timing rather than calling quiet participants unprepared. The inquiry asks whether the arrangement produces useful evidence for the decision.

items.title: A change that looks easy
items.body: Sending a draft earlier may help, but only if it is approved for the intended recipients and questions go to a responsible owner. Confirm version and access before sharing. A learning metaphor cannot authorize private-document disclosure or convert an informal discussion into required formal review.

items.title: An extra route without a response
items.body: A written channel can collect comments that no one reads before the decision. Then the visible accommodation of another style has little practical value. Assign the response role and check how concerns are examined. The benefit should be a usable contribution, not merely a second link in the invitation.

tabs.label: Person explanation
tabs.body: Explaining quietness as a trait may leave the meeting unchanged. The team can keep asking for immediate responses while blaming people who cannot use the arrangement. A better inquiry considers the task and format before interpreting a person’s contribution or assigning a group preference.

tabs.label: Process assumption
tabs.body: A process assumption names what the arrangement expects, such as immediate access to the meaning of a long draft. It can be checked through instructions, timing and work evidence. This approach often needs less personal information and places improvement with the staff who control the arrangement.

tabs.label: Practical option
tabs.body: A practical option connects the assumption to an authorized response with an owner. Earlier permitted draft access can create review time; a written route can preserve questions. Explain how the route works and check whether the decision used it. Added choice without follow-through may simply add work.

check.question: In this example, a team wants a written review channel after noticing few meeting comments. What must it consider?
check.correct: The decision purpose, permitted material access, response owner and how questions will be examined before the choice closes.
wrong: Which employee identity should automatically require written responses.
Whether course learning allows bypassing private-document permissions.
Whether a second channel counts as success even if nobody checks it.
check.feedbackCorrect: This develops a usable process option while preserving responsibility and an evidence-based result check.
check.feedbackIncorrect: An identity rule substitutes an assumed group preference for individual choice. The course does not alter document permissions. A channel no one checks may provide no meaningful influence. Connect the option to actual work, authorized access and a response owner before calling it an improvement.

items.text: Participants can examine every long draft instantly.
Confirm permitted recipients before sharing the draft.
Quiet participants lack the right culture for the team.
Everyone knows which mailbox receives comments.
Assign who examines comments before the decision.
A presumed identity always determines the response method.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: A practice workgroup offers an additional written comment link but leaves it unchecked until after the policy choice. Lead Jordan reports that the process is now culturally inclusive because a second channel exists.
options: Make a personal cultural score for people who used the link.
Explain the work question, assign an authorized response owner and check whether the route can influence the still-open decision.
Keep the route symbolic because choice alone proves success.
responses: Channel use cannot establish an individual orientation or a personnel score.
This turns the option into usable decision participation within its actual limits.
A choice without examination or response may not meet the claimed purpose.

lessons.transfer: Use a practice process iceberg: visible arrangement, underlying assumption, evidence question, authorized option, owner and usefulness check.

move.control: You can examine a process you touch and choose a supported improvement within authority.
move.failure: The picture locates the problem entirely inside other people while the arrangement remains unusable.
move.next: Point the next iceberg inquiry toward one workplace default before asking for anyone’s personal explanation.

intro.heading: Review the inquiry and state what remains unknown
intro.body:
A useful iceberg inquiry should change the quality of a question or response. At the end, describe the observation, the initial interpretation, the evidence you examined and what you now understand differently. This account lets another reader assess the reasoning. A completed diagram alone does not show learning or justify an action.

In a practice review, a quiet participant later explains that the draft arrived during the meeting and contained an unresolved source comparison. The team provides earlier approved material and a clear response route. In the next review, a useful source question reaches the owner before the choice closes. You can describe that process change and its result. You cannot say that every participant’s culture was understood or that all barriers disappeared.

Keep nonresponse and other limits visible. Some participants may not answer a follow-up question, and timing may not be the only influence on the result. Do not fill the lower section with reassurance or an assumed negative attitude. A missing account remains missing. Use appropriate, minimal work evidence and avoid turning optional practice into a hidden employee commitment or IDI measure.

Choose the next responsible action. Continue a useful route, repair a remaining instruction gap or seek guidance about an issue outside your authority. Formal concerns retain their designated processes; managers and supervisors must immediately report covered discrimination or harassment allegations to HR or the affirmative action officer under MMB policy. The diagram does not replace those duties. Staff retain ownership of their inquiry and can use consultant feedback to strengthen it without requiring a consultant to perform the work.

inThisLesson: Summarize a practice inquiry with observation, evidence and revised interpretation.
Distinguish a useful work result from a universal cultural claim.
Choose follow-through that preserves evidence limits and formal responsibilities.
What should the summary include?
lessons.keyStatement: Finish with a supported account and a next step, not a claim to have uncovered someone’s entire culture.

items.title: The explanation changed
items.body: An initial disengagement label becomes an account of late material and an unresolved evidence question. Explain what information changed the interpretation. That does not establish the only cause of every response; it shows a better-supported explanation and a practical process action for this case.

items.title: The diagram is complete
items.body: Every box contains text, but some statements are still guesses. Completion does not convert them into findings. Mark observations, supported accounts and open questions distinctly. An honestly incomplete inquiry is more useful than a polished image that hides uncertainty or makes a personal developmental claim.

items.title: A formal issue emerges
items.body: A learning question can reveal a concern with designated responsibilities. Preserve that route rather than keeping the concern in the picture for further reflection. A manager’s immediate reporting duty is not delayed by the inquiry. Appropriate practical support can continue without a course-based investigation or finding.

tabs.label: Supported account
tabs.body: A supported account explains the observation and the evidence that changed an interpretation. If a participant lacked the draft, the account can describe that barrier and the response. It should not expand into a claim about every community member or omit evidence that points to another relevant condition.

tabs.label: Open question
tabs.body: An open question identifies what the inquiry has not established. Nonresponse may reflect several conditions, and the diagram cannot select one automatically. Stating the gap helps choose the next proportionate check. It also prevents missing data from being presented as satisfaction, resistance or a developmental result.

tabs.label: Follow-through
tabs.body: Follow-through checks the practical action and preserves responsibility. Did the permitted draft arrive earlier, did questions reach an owner and did they receive a response? That result can guide another process improvement. A separate formal concern still follows its designated route rather than being closed by a successful meeting.

check.question: What is the strongest final statement after a practice iceberg inquiry?
check.correct: Earlier permitted draft access helped one source question reach the owner before the decision; other responses and causes remain unexamined.
wrong: The complete diagram proves every employee’s culture is understood.
The activity provides an individual IDI result for each participant.
check.feedbackCorrect: The statement describes a bounded work result and makes the remaining evidence limits visible.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A completed diagram does not establish universal understanding. Nonresponse cannot reassure you that there are no concerns. This activity does not administer or infer IDI results. Describe the actual change, the appropriate evidence and the remaining questions, then follow the responsibilities that apply.

items.text: A useful question reached the decision owner through the revised route.
The reasons for several missing responses remain unknown.
The diagram proves all cultural barriers are gone.
The approved draft was available before the next review.
Other changes may also have affected participation.
Each participant receives an inferred IDI score.

lessons.next: Use the job aid to observe carefully, check meaning and make a responsible practical response.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: In this example, a team completes iceberg diagrams and changes its review timing. One important evidence question arrives before the decision. Several participants do not respond to a follow-up, but leader Priya wants to announce that every barrier is gone.
options: A universal success statement because the team worked hard.
A negative commitment score for people who did not respond.
The observed route change and useful question, the missing evidence and an owned next check without personal assessment claims.
responses: Effort and diagram completion do not establish every person’s experience or permanent success.
Missing responses do not identify attitude, commitment or developmental orientation.
This makes the practical learning visible while keeping the account accurate and actionable.

lessons.transfer: Write a practice inquiry summary with observation, initial interpretation, checked evidence, revised account, work result, limit and next responsibility.

move.control: You can report learning and improve work while remaining clear about uncertainty and duties.
move.failure: A completed metaphor becomes an unsupported success claim or personal assessment.
move.next: Review the next inquiry for evidence, scope and follow-through before sharing its conclusion.

jobAid.subtitle: Use the image to organize an inquiry, not to label a person.
remember: The iceberg is a metaphor, not a percentage measure or personal assessment.
Describe the surface before inventing what is below it.
A process assumption may be more useful to examine than a private identity account.

sections.heading: Describe and distinguish
items: Write the observable action or arrangement with relevant context.
Separate the effect from a motive or trait claim.
Name your interpretation as an interpretation.
Keep the meaning of another person’s account appropriately scoped.

sections.heading: Ask and examine
items: Consider more than one plausible explanation.
Choose a neutral task question or proportionate evidence check.
Distinguish cultural meaning, information gaps, access needs and formal concerns.

sections.heading: Respond and review
items: Compare an option with the work purpose and actual authority.
Assign an appropriate owner and response route.
Describe the work result and missing evidence honestly.
Do not infer an individual IDI orientation or create a hidden personnel score.
Preserve designated duties and formal procedures when concerns arise.

sources.title: Peace Corps — Culture Is Like an Iceberg
sources.note: Primary educational example of the visible/less apparent metaphor. This course does not copy its worksheets or apply a physical iceberg percentage as a measurement of culture.

sources.title: Council of Europe — Developing intercultural competence through education
sources.note: Educational reference for context, multiple affiliations and internal cultural variation. The original DHS practice cases do not establish individual or group traits.

sources.title: IDI — Intercultural Development Continuum
sources.note: Official five-orientation reference. The iceberg activity is not an IDI assessment or a way to infer someone’s orientation.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — Harassment and Discrimination Prohibited
sources.note: Actual manager and supervisor immediate reporting duties remain in effect; a learning inquiry does not replace formal handling.
